h: A Royal Spa Town with Rocks to Climb
p: North Farm sits on the north-eastern side of town, near High Brooms, and it's a handy spot to get to from the A21. Once you've finished jumping, a quick drive into the centre opens up one of the most elegant towns in Kent.

Tunbridge Wells owes its whole existence to water. In 1606, Lord North discovered an iron-rich spring here, and visitors soon flocked to drink it for their health. The chalybeate spring can still be found at the end of the Pantiles, and you can see where the town's fashionable past began. The Royal part of the name came later, granted by Edward VII in 1909.

Just west of the centre, the sandstone outcrops around Rusthall and High Rocks are a big hit with kids. Toad Rock, a huge rock that looks uncannily like a giant toad, is a local landmark and great for a photo.
Train fans have a treat in store, too. The Spa Valley Railway runs heritage trains from Tunbridge Wells West to Eridge, with steam and diesel engines and special events through the year.

In the town centre, Calverley Grounds is a pleasant green space for a run-around, while Groombridge Place, a short drive away, has gardens and woodland to explore. Bewl Water, a big reservoir to the south-east, is ideal for walks and cycling on a fine day.
Tunbridge Wells is hilly and the centre gets busy at weekends, so park once and walk between the Pantiles and the shops. It's a lovely way to slow the pace after a high-energy session.
